npm postinstall hook spawning a shell interpreter on a developer device AIInstallation High
Catches the article's exact execution chain: node/npm running a postinstall/preinstall script that immediately spawns cmd, PowerShell, bash, sh, or wscript/cscript/mshta — the textbook supply-chain payload pattern flagged by the Aikido advisory. Rationale: Targets the article's literal execution narrative: 'pulls a new dependency, executes the postinstall hook' — node/npm as the spawner, shell as the child. Parent-cmdline filter pins it to install-hook context, not interactive node use. Kill-chain Phase 2 detection hint.
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1204.002 T1546.016
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • node-gyp / node-pre-gyp native module compile scripts (legitimate cmd.exe / sh.exe spawn during install of e.g. bcrypt, sharp)
  • Electron / Playwright postinstall downloading browser binaries with curl
  • Husky git-hook installer spawning a shell during `npm install`
  • Lerna / nx monorepo install orchestrators running cross-package scripts
  • Yarn berry's `node-modules` linker reorganising .bin shims
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp","node-pre-gyp","prebuild-install","husky","playwright install","electron install","puppeteer")) and not (FolderPath has "\\node_modules\\bcrypt\\" or FolderPath has "\\node_modules\\sharp\\")
Response runbook
1. Triage: capture the full parent + child command lines and the package whose postinstall fired (resolve from node_modules path); is this a known native-build module (node-gyp/sharp/bcrypt) or an unknown package? 2. Contain: isolate the host, terminate the descendent chain, suspend the developer's npm publish token and any GitHub PATs scoped to the device. 3. Hunt: pivot on the package name across the fleet via DeviceFileEvents writes to node_modules; check DeviceNetworkEvents from the host in the 5 minutes after the shell spawned for the article's C2 IPs/domains; check Slack audit logs for an AI-agent-approved PR that pulled the dependency.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("postinstall","preinstall","install.js","install.cjs","node_modules\\.bin")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","curl.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
  ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
  ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
  ChildImage  = FolderPath,
  ChildCmd    = ProcessCommandLine,
  SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node.exe","npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe")
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("postinstall","preinstall","install.js","install.cjs","node_modules")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","curl.exe","certutil.exe")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: npm Postinstall Hook Spawning a Shell Interpreter
id: a1f2c3d4-5e6f-47a8-9b1c-2d3e4f5a6b7c
description: Detects node/npm/yarn/pnpm spawning cmd, PowerShell, bash, sh, wscript, cscript, mshta, curl, or certutil during a postinstall/preinstall hook on a developer workstation.
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering

tags:

logsource:

detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\node.exe'
      - '\npm.exe'
      - '\yarn.exe'
      - '\pnpm.exe'
    ParentCommandLine|contains:
      - 'postinstall'
      - 'preinstall'
      - 'install.js'
      - 'install.cjs'
      - 'node_modules'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\cmd.exe'

      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'

source:(windows.sysmon OR windows.security) @EventID:(1 OR 4688) @ParentImage:(*\\node.exe OR *\\NODE.EXE OR *\\npm.exe OR *\\NPM.EXE OR *\\yarn.exe OR *\\YARN.EXE OR *\\pnpm.exe OR *\\PNPM.EXE) @ParentCommandLine:(*postinstall* OR *preinstall* OR *install.js* OR *install.cjs* OR *node_modules*) @Image:(*\\cmd.exe OR *\\CMD.EXE OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\POWERSHELL.EXE OR *\\pwsh.exe OR *\\bash.exe OR *\\sh.exe OR *\\wscript.exe OR *\\WSCRIPT.EXE OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\CSCRIPT.EXE OR *\\mshta.exe OR *\\MSHTA.EXE OR *\\curl.exe OR *\\certutil.exe OR *\\bitsadmin.exe)

| regex("postinstall|preinstall|install\\.cjs|install\\.js|node_modules", field=ParentImageFileName) OR regex("postinstall|preinstall|install\\.cjs|install\\.js|node_modules", field=CommandLine)
| ImageFileName=/(cmd|powershell|pwsh|bash|sh|wscript|cscript|mshta|curl|certutil|bitsadmin)\.exe$/i

Execution of binaries matching Aikido article SHA1 hashes AIInstallation Medium
Hard-IOC sweep for the three SHA1 hashes (2553649f..., d6f3f62f..., 07d889e2...) tied by Aikido Intel to the GlassWorm / TeamPCP / postmark-mcp postinstall payloads. Triggers on either process execution or file landing. Rationale: Three SHA1 hashes are explicit hard IOCs published alongside the article — zero-FP signal when matched. Kill-chain Phase 2 explicitly lists these hashes. Worth a 90-day retrospective sweep on first deploy.
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher re-analysing the IOCs in a sandbox
  • Threat-intel team detonating the sample in an isolated detonation VM
  • Incident-response retained artifact already known-quarantined by Defender
  • EDR vendor's own validation hash test on a security-team device
Response runbook
1. Triage: confirm the hit isn't from a known security-research sandbox or AV vendor test machine; pull file path, signer, parent process. 2. Contain: isolate the host immediately, take a memory image before reboot, revoke all secrets reachable from the developer's home directory (AWS, npm, GitHub PATs, kubeconfig, Bitwarden vault), force-rotate the developer's SSO password and reset MFA. 3. Hunt: pivot on the parent npm package name fleet-wide; check the kill-chain C2 IPs/domains in DeviceNetworkEvents from the host going back 90 days; review GitHub audit log for the developer's PAT for bulk-clone activity.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca","d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71","07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766"]);
union
  (DeviceProcessEvents
   | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
   | where SHA1 in (BadHashes) or InitiatingProcessSHA1 in (BadHashes)
   | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA1, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, Source="Process"),
  (DeviceFileEvents
   | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
   | where SHA1 in (BadHashes)
   | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA1, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, Source="File")
| order by Timestamp desc
let BadHashes = dynamic(["2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca","d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71","07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766"]);
union
  (ImProcessCreate
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
   | where SHA1 in (BadHashes)
   | project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA1, Source="Process"),
  (ImFileEvent
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
   | where TargetFileSHA1 in (BadHashes)
   | project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName=ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA1=TargetFileSHA1, TargetFileName, Source="File")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Developer-host beacon to GlassWorm / TeamPCP C2 infrastructure AICommand & Control High
Outbound network or DNS from any endpoint to the four C2 IPs (142.11.206.73, 45.32.150.251, 45.32.151.157, 70.34.242.255) or the two domains (giftshop.club, sfrclak.com) named in the article. Highest priority when the initiating process is node/npm/Code.exe. Rationale: Six hard network IOCs (4 IPs + 2 domains) from kill-chain Phase 6 — direct match against the Aikido article's C2 list. Enrichment flag on node.exe / Code.exe / browser process owner identifies the developer-device pivot the article calls out.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel ingestion job pre-fetching the IOCs for sandboxing
  • Web filter / proxy testing the IOC list with active probes
  • Researcher visiting giftshop.club via a controlled browser
  • Defender ASR test traffic
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("misp-feed.exe","otx-fetcher.exe","threatfox-sync.exe") and DeviceName !startswith "TI-SANDBOX-"
Response runbook
1. Triage: identify the source device, the initiating process tree, and whether the traffic was blocked at proxy/firewall vs allowed. 2. Contain: isolate the device via EDR, sinkhole the domains at the recursive resolver, block the IPs at egress, force-revoke all secrets reachable from the developer's home directory (AWS, npm, GitHub PATs, Bitwarden, kubeconfig). 3. Hunt: retro-sweep 90 days of DeviceNetworkEvents and DNS across the fleet for the same IOCs; cross-reference with kill-chain Phase 1 IOC package installs on the same hosts in the prior 24h.
let BadIPs = dynamic(["142.11.206.73","45.32.150.251","45.32.151.157","70.34.242.255"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["giftshop.club","sfrclak.com"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where RemoteIP in (BadIPs)
   or RemoteUrl has_any (BadDomains)
| extend Suspect_NodeOrIDE = InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","Code.exe","electron.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, Suspect_NodeOrIDE
| order by Timestamp desc
let BadIPs = dynamic(["142.11.206.73","45.32.150.251","45.32.151.157","70.34.242.255"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["giftshop.club","sfrclak.com"]);
union
  (ImNetworkSession
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
   | where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   | project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, Src=SrcHostname, SrcUser=SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, Url, AppProto=NetworkApplicationProtocol, Source="Network"),
  (ImDnsActivity
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
   | where DnsQuery has_any (BadDomains)
   | project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, Src=SrcHostname, SrcUser=SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstHostname=tostring(DnsResponseName), DstPortNumber=int(null), Url=tostring(DnsQuery), AppProto="dns", Source="DNS")
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Beacon to GlassWorm / TeamPCP C2 Infrastructure
id: c4d5e6f7-8a9b-4c0d-1e2f-3a4b5c6d7e8f
description: Detects outbound connections or DNS queries from any endpoint to the C2 IPs and domains published in the Aikido June 2026 advisory.
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/10
tags:

  - attack.command_and_control
logsource:
  category: network_connection
  product: windows
detection:

      - '142.11.206.73'
      - '45.32.150.251'
      - '45.32.151.157'
      - '70.34.242.255'
  selection_domain:
    DestinationHostname|contains:
      - 'giftshop.club'
      - 'sfrclak.com'

(source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 (@DestinationIp:(142.11.206.73 OR 45.32.150.251 OR 45.32.151.157 OR 70.34.242.255) OR @DestinationHostname:(*giftshop.club* OR *sfrclak.com*))) OR (source:windows.sysmon @EventID:22 @QueryName:(*giftshop.club* OR *sfrclak.com*))
(#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 (RemoteAddressIP4="142.11.206.73" OR RemoteAddressIP4="45.32.150.251" OR RemoteAddressIP4="45.32.151.157" OR RemoteAddressIP4="70.34.242.255"))
OR (#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/giftshop\.club|sfrclak\.com/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, DomainName], function=count())

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_ip IN ("142.11.206.73","45.32.150.251","45.32.151.157","70.34.242.255") OR All_Traffic.dest IN ("giftshop.club","sfrclak.com") OR All_Traffic.url="*giftshop.club*" OR All_Traffic.url="*sfrclak.com*" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.src_user All_Traffic.dest_ip All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

Postinstall-driven read of cloud credentials and SSH keys from developer home AIActions on Objectives Medium
A node/npm-spawned process reading ~/.aws/credentials, ~/.ssh/id_*, ~/.npmrc, ~/.kube/config or a Bitwarden vault file — the credential-theft step the article describes ('cloud credentials, SSH keys, npm publish tokens, Kubernetes configs'). Rationale: Pairs the article's named credential stores (cloud creds, SSH keys, npm tokens, kubeconfig) with node.exe parent — high-signal because legitimate node code rarely reads ~/.aws/credentials or ~/.ssh/id_* during a postinstall. Kill-chain Phase 4 detection hint.
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1555 T1528
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • aws-sdk-js / aws-vault helper modules legitimately reading ~/.aws/credentials at runtime
  • ssh2 / simple-git npm modules reading ~/.ssh/id_rsa for repo auth during a build
  • kubectl-node wrapper modules reading ~/.kube/config
  • Bitwarden CLI legitimate authenticated session refresh
  • Developer running `npm login` writes .npmrc
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("aws-sdk","aws-vault","@kubernetes/client-node","simple-git","node-ssh","ssh2")) and not (FolderPath has "\\node_modules\\@aws-sdk\\")
Response runbook
1. Triage: identify the npm package whose postinstall touched the credential file (walk the InitiatingProcessParentId chain) — is the package on the Aikido IOC list? 2. Contain: rotate every credential that lived in the touched files (AWS keys, SSH keys + replace authorized_keys, npm publish tokens, kubeconfig tokens, Bitwarden master password); isolate the host; pull memory before reboot. 3. Hunt: check CloudTrail / Azure AD / GitHub audit logs for use of those credentials from any IP not previously seen for the developer's identity in the prior 30 days.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
   or ActionType has "Open"
| where (FolderPath has_any (@"\.aws\credentials", @"\.aws\config", @"\.ssh\", @"\.npmrc", @"\.kube\config", @"Bitwarden\data.json", @"@bitwarden\")
     or FileName in~ ("credentials","id_rsa","id_ed25519","id_ecdsa",".npmrc","kubeconfig","data.json",".env"))
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","Code.exe","electron.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("postinstall","preinstall","node_modules","install.js")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType,
  InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
  InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where (TargetFilePath has_any ("/.aws/credentials","/.aws/config","/.ssh/","/.npmrc","/.kube/config","Bitwarden\\data.json","@bitwarden")
     or TargetFileName in~ ("credentials","id_rsa","id_ed25519","id_ecdsa",".npmrc","kubeconfig","data.json",".env"))
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node.exe","npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("postinstall","preinstall","node_modules","install.js","install.cjs")
   or ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Host=DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:(windows.sysmon OR linux.auditd) (@EventID:11 OR @auditd.type:PATH) (@TargetFilename:(*\\.aws\\credentials* OR *\\.aws\\config* OR *\\.ssh\\id_* OR *\\.npmrc* OR *\\.kube\\config* OR *Bitwarden\\data.json* OR *.env) OR @file.path:(*/.aws/credentials* OR */.ssh/id_* OR */.npmrc* OR */.kube/config*)) @Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\NODE.EXE OR *\\npm.exe OR *\\NPM.EXE OR */bin/node OR */bin/npm)
(#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo OR #event_simpleName=FileWritten)
| ContextImageFileName=/(node|npm|yarn|pnpm)\.exe$/i
| regex("\\\\\\.aws\\\\credentials|\\\\\\.aws\\\\config|\\\\\\.ssh\\\\id_|\\\\\\.npmrc|\\\\\\.kube\\\\config|Bitwarden\\\\data\\.json|@bitwarden|\\\\\\.env", field=TargetFileName)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.process_name IN ("node.exe","npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe") (Filesystem.file_path="*\\.aws\\credentials*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\.aws\\config*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\.ssh\\id_*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\.npmrc*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\.kube\\config*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Bitwarden*\\data.json*" OR Filesystem.file_name=".env") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.process_name IN ("node.exe","npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe") (Filesystem.file_path="*\\.aws\\credentials*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\.aws\\config*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\.ssh\\id_*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\.npmrc*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\.kube\\config*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\Bitwarden*\\data.json*" OR Filesystem.file_name=".env") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or SHA1 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or MD5 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or SHA1 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766") or MD5 in~ ("2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["2553649f2322049666871cea80a5d0d6adc700ca", "d6f3f62fd3b9f5432f5782b62d8cfd5247d5ee71", "07d889e2dadce6f3910dcbc253317d28ca61c766"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Oracle PeopleSoft servers hacked in ShinyHunters data theft attacks

BleepingComputer
2026-06-10 11 use cases 2 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Oracle PeopleSoft servers are being targeted in ongoing data theft attacks by the ShinyHunters extortion gang, which claims to have stolen data from over 100 organizations. [...]

ATT&CKT1190 T1195.002
Domainsazurenetfiles.net
IPs142.11.200.186 142.11.200.187 142.11.200.188 142.11.200.189 142.11.200.190 108.174.202.99 176.120.22.24

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Network communication with ShinyHunters PeopleSoft attack infrastructure IPs
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] SSH credential spray against PeopleSoft administrative accounts (psoft, oracle, linuxadm) · [LLM] MeshCentral agent installation on Oracle PeopleSoft Linux servers · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Oracle PeopleSoft servers hacked in ShinyHunters data theft attacks
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] DNS lookup or TLS SNI for ShinyHunters azurenetfiles.net infrastructure · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] ShinyHunters PeopleSoft ransom-note file write (README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED.TXT) · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Network communication with ShinyHunters PeopleSoft attack infrastructure IPs AIDelivery Medium
Hunts for any inbound or outbound network traffic to the seven IPs Michael R recovered from exposed ShinyHunters staging directories. The article tells operators to analyse logs for connections from these IPs to PeopleSoft instances — this is the primary IOC pivot. Rationale: Anchored on the seven IPs published by Michael R and re-shared by BleepingComputer. Several of these IPs presented the azurenetfiles.net TLS certificate, a known ShinyHunters infrastructure marker. Cross-checked the abuse.ch IP intel feed and BleepingComputer's prior ShinyHunters coverage tying azurenetfiles.net to the group. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/oracle-peoplesoft-servers-hacked-in-shinyhunters-data-theft-attacks/ • https://threatfox.abuse.ch/ • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1015/
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel feed scrapers proxying through your egress (e.g. researcher VMs polling sinkholes)
  • Internal vulnerability scans that include the IPs as part of an external-attack-surface sweep
  • Legitimate web traffic if any IP is shared with a CDN PoP in the future (currently dedicated)
  • VPN concentrators forwarding telemetry to threat-intel platforms
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","SenseIR.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "threatintel"
Response runbook
1. Triage: pivot on DeviceName/host receiving traffic — confirm it is an Oracle PeopleSoft web, app, or batch server. Pull the full process tree around the connection time and any HTTP requests in W3CIISLog / WebLogic / Tuxedo access logs to identify the exploited endpoint. 2. Contain: pull the host off internet routing (firewall block + remove from load balancer), preserve memory and disk, rotate the psoft / oracle / linuxadm credentials and any SSH keys present, and revoke all PeopleSoft active sessions. 3. Hunt: search for the ShinyHunters ransom note filename, MeshCentral binaries/agents, outbound DNS to azurenetfiles.net, and SSH activity from the PeopleSoft host to internal hosts named in /etc/hosts.

ShinyHunters PeopleSoft ransom-note file write (README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED.TXT) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects creation of the specific ransom-note filename the ShinyHunters script drops on compromised PeopleSoft web and application servers. The name is unique enough to alert on directly with effectively zero false positives. Rationale: The article reproduces the exact filename the ShinyHunters shell script writes — 'README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED.TXT'. The string is long, unique, all-caps with hyphens and verbs, so an exact file-create match is high-fidelity and effectively unhittable by legitimate software. Cross-checked the screenshot at https://www.bleepstatic.com/images/news/security/attacks/p/peoplesoft/shinyhunters/shiny-script.jpg. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/oracle-peoplesoft-servers-hacked-in-shinyhunters-data-theft-attacks/
ATT&CKT1657 T1486 T1565.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IR team or threat-intel analyst copying the IOC into a local file for hunt enrichment
  • Detection-engineering tests deploying a benign decoy with the same name
  • EDR sandbox detonating the ShinyHunters script in an isolated lab
  • Forensic image mounted on an analyst workstation containing a previously-dropped note
Response runbook
1. Triage: identify the host writing the note and the writing process — for a Linux PeopleSoft server this should be bash/sh invoked from an SSH session. Capture the .bash_history of the writing user. 2. Contain: immediately isolate the host, snapshot the disk, rotate the writing user's SSH keys and password, and revoke any cached PeopleSoft application credentials. 3. Hunt: search peer PeopleSoft hosts (peers from /etc/hosts) for the same filename, any SSH logons from the original compromised host outbound, and network egress to the seven ShinyHunters IPs in the prior UC.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed")
| where FileName =~ "README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED.TXT"
   or FolderPath has "README-IF-YOU-SEE-THIS-YOUVE-BEEN-HACKED.TXT"

SSH credential spray against PeopleSoft administrative accounts (psoft, oracle, linuxadm) AIInstallation High
Detects SSH authentication attempts targeting the three accounts the ShinyHunters lateral-movement script enumerates. The script tries password auth first then falls back to keys, so we alert on a single source generating both successful AND failed auth events against any of these usernames within a short window. Rationale: Article describes the script parsing /etc/hosts to find PeopleSoft hosts and attempting SSH with exactly these three usernames — psoft, oracle, linuxadm — before falling back to key-based auth. The username triplet plus multi-host fan-out is article-specific and not a generic SSH brute-force template. Cross-checked Oracle PeopleSoft installation guides confirming 'psoft' and 'oracle' as the standard install accounts. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/oracle-peoplesoft-servers-hacked-in-shinyhunters-data-theft-attacks/ • https://docs.oracle.com/cd/F36211_01/psft/pdf/PT859TIBM-b1119.pdf
ATT&CKT1110.003 T1078.003 T1021.004
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Ansible/Chef/Puppet runs using the oracle account against multiple PeopleSoft hosts in the same batch window
  • Backup tooling (rsync, RMAN) authenticating as oracle to peer hosts
  • DBA bastion-host shell sessions hopping between PeopleSoft tier-1 and tier-2 servers
  • PeopleSoft application-server restart playbooks that SSH into every web tier
  • Pentest exercises authorised by the customer
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("ansible","puppet","chef-client","saltstack","rmanbackup")
Response runbook
1. Triage: enumerate the source IP — confirm whether it is internal (compromised peer) or external. If internal, treat that host as already-breached; if external, cross-reference against the seven IOC IPs. Pull historical successful logons for the same source across the prior 30 days. 2. Contain: rotate the password and SSH key material for psoft / oracle / linuxadm on every PeopleSoft host (and any host where these accounts also exist). Disable password authentication on PeopleSoft sshd_config if not already done. Add firewall rules restricting SSH ingress to bastion-only. 3. Hunt: review .bash_history of all three accounts on every targeted host, look for the ShinyHunters ransom-note filename, and check whether /etc/hosts itself was read by an unusual process (cat/grep/awk parented by sshd or bash from an external SSH session).
DeviceLogonEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where Protocol =~ "Ssh" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("sshd","sshd-session")
| where AccountName in~ ("psoft","oracle","linuxadm")
| summarize Attempts = count(),
            Successes = countif(ActionType =~ "LogonSuccess"),
            Failures = countif(ActionType =~ "LogonFailed"),
            TargetHosts = dcount(DeviceName),
            HostList = make_set(DeviceName, 25),
            UserList = make_set(AccountName, 10),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp),
            LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
            by RemoteIP
| where TargetHosts >= 2 or (Failures >= 5 and Successes >= 1)
| order by LastSeen desc
let badIPs = dynamic(["142.11.200.186","142.11.200.187","142.11.200.188","142.11.200.189","142.11.200.190","108.174.202.99","176.120.22.24"]);
let psoftAccounts = dynamic(["psoft","oracle","linuxadm"]);
union isfuzzy=true
  (Syslog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
    | where Facility in ("auth","authpriv") or ProcessName =~ "sshd"
    | where SyslogMessage has_any (psoftAccounts)
    | extend User = extract(@"(?i)user[= ]([A-Za-z0-9._-]+)", 1, SyslogMessage),
             SrcIP = extract(@"from\s+([0-9a-f:.]+)", 1, SyslogMessage),
             Outcome = case(SyslogMessage has "Accepted", "success", SyslogMessage has_any ("Failed","Invalid user","authentication failure"), "failure", "other")
    | where User in~ (psoftAccounts)
    | project TimeGenerated, Host = Computer, User, SrcIP, Outcome, SyslogMessage),
  (ImAuthentication
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
    | where LogonProtocol =~ "SSH" or EventProduct =~ "OpenSSH" or TargetAppName =~ "sshd"
    | where TargetUsername in~ (psoftAccounts)
    | project TimeGenerated, Host = DvcHostname, User = TargetUsername, SrcIP = SrcIpAddr, Outcome = EventResult, SyslogMessage = EventResultDetails)
| summarize Attempts = count(),
            Successes = countif(Outcome =~ "success" or Outcome =~ "Success"),
            Failures = countif(Outcome =~ "failure" or Outcome =~ "Failure"),
            TargetHosts = dcount(Host),
            HostList = make_set(Host, 25),
            UserList = make_set(User, 5),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
            by SrcIP
| where TargetHosts >= 2 or (Failures >= 5 and Successes >= 1) or SrcIP in (badIPs)
| order by LastSeen desc
(source:linux.syslog OR source:linux.auditd OR source:okta) (@process.name:sshd OR @SyslogFacility:auth OR @evt.name:user.session.start) (@usr.id:(psoft OR oracle OR linuxadm) OR @user.name:(psoft OR oracle OR linuxadm) OR @TargetUsername:(psoft OR oracle OR linuxadm) OR @actor.alternateId:(psoft OR oracle OR linuxadm))
#event_simpleName=UserLogon
| LogonType=Network OR LogonType=Interactive OR LogonType=RemoteInteractive OR AuthenticationPackage=/ssh/i
| in(field=UserName, values=["psoft","oracle","linuxadm"]) OR in(field=RemoteAccount, values=["psoft","oracle","linuxadm"])
| groupBy([RemoteAddressIP4, UserName], function={
    count() as Attempts,
    count(field=aid, distinct=true) as TargetHostCount,
    min(_time) as FirstSeen,
    max(_time) as LastSeen
  })
| TargetHostCount >= 2
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count values(Authentication.action) as actions values(Authentication.dest) as dest_hosts dc(Authentication.dest) as host_count dc(Authentication.user) as user_count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.app="sshd" AND Authentication.user IN ("psoft","oracle","linuxadm") by Authentication.src Authentication.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where host_count>=2 OR (user_count>=2) | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count values(Authentication.action) as actions values(Authentication.dest) as dest_hosts dc(Authentication.dest) as host_count dc(Authentication.user) as user_count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.app="sshd" AND Authentication.user IN ("psoft","oracle","linuxadm") by Authentication.src Authentication.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where host_count>=2 OR (user_count>=2) | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
MeshCentral agent installation on Oracle PeopleSoft Linux servers AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for MeshCentral remote-management agent binaries or service installs on hosts identifying as PeopleSoft servers. The ShinyHunters staging directory included MeshCentral agents, indicating the actor uses MeshCentral as a backdoor / RMM C2 channel rather than dropping bespoke malware. Rationale: The article explicitly says Michael R found MeshCentral agents in the exposed ShinyHunters staging directories. MeshCentral binaries and command-line flags such as --meshServiceName / meshcentral.com beaconing are documented in the public MeshCentral source. We hunt rather than alert because MeshCentral is also a legitimate RMM — cross-checked the MeshCentral project documentation and the abuse.ch URLhaus listings for MeshCentral C2 panels. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/oracle-peoplesoft-servers-hacked-in-shinyhunters-data-theft-attacks/ • https://github.com/Ylianst/MeshCentral • https://urlhaus.abuse.ch/
ATT&CKT1219 T1543.002 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT operations using MeshCentral as a sanctioned RMM tool for endpoint management
  • Schools running MeshCentral student-lab management (article notes education is most-affected sector)
  • Vendor support technicians authorised to remote into PeopleSoft tier servers via MeshCentral
  • Existing detection-engineering or red-team test environments running MeshCentral as part of C2 lab exercises
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("itops-","helpdesk-","rmm-") and InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("sccm","ansible","itadmin"))
Response runbook
1. Triage: identify whether MeshCentral is an approved tool in this environment (ask IT). If approved, verify the install path, parent process, and the configured server domain match the sanctioned deployment. If unapproved or pointing at azurenetfiles.net / one of the seven IOC IPs, treat as confirmed C2. 2. Contain: kill the meshagent process, remove the systemd unit / Windows service, block the agent's configured server IP and azurenetfiles.net at the perimeter, snapshot the host, and rotate all local credentials. 3. Hunt: enumerate every host where the meshagent binary or its install path exists, pivot the agent's server hostname against DNS logs org-wide, and check for the ShinyHunters ransom-note file and SSH key-based logons to the same host.
let MeshIndicators = dynamic(["meshagent","meshservice","meshcmd","meshcentral","meshcentral.com","meshcentral2"]);
union
  (DeviceProcessEvents
   | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
   | where FileName in~ ("meshagent","meshagent.exe","meshservice","meshservice.exe","meshcmd","meshcmd.exe")
        or ProcessCommandLine has_any (MeshIndicators)
        or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (MeshIndicators)
   | project Timestamp, EventType = "Process", DeviceName, AccountName,
             Image = FolderPath, Cmd = ProcessCommandLine,
             ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256),
  (DeviceFileEvents
   | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
   | where FileName in~ ("meshagent","meshagent.exe","meshservice","meshservice.exe","meshcmd")
        or FolderPath has_any ("/usr/local/mesh","/opt/meshcentral","meshagent","MeshCentral")
   | project Timestamp, EventType = "File", DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName,
             Image = FolderPath, Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
             ParentImage = InitiatingProcessParentFileName, ParentCmd = "", SHA256)
| order by Timestamp desc
let MeshIndicators = dynamic(["meshagent","meshservice","meshcmd","meshcentral","meshcentral.com","meshcentral2"]);
union isfuzzy=true
  (ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where ActingProcessName has_any (MeshIndicators) or TargetProcessName has_any (MeshIndicators) or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (MeshIndicators) or TargetProcessCommandLine has_any (MeshIndicators)
    | project TimeGenerated, _Source = "ImProcessCreate", Host = DvcHostname, User = ActorUsername, Image = TargetProcessName, Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentImage = ActingProcessName, ParentCmd = ActingProcessCommandLine),
  (ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where TargetFileName has_any (MeshIndicators) or TargetFilePath has_any ("/usr/local/mesh","/opt/meshcentral","meshagent","MeshCentral")
    | project TimeGenerated, _Source = "ImFileEvent", Host = DvcHostname, User = ActorUsername, Image = TargetFilePath, Cmd = ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentImage = ActingProcessName, ParentCmd = ""),
  (Syslog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where SyslogMessage has_any (MeshIndicators)
    | project TimeGenerated, _Source = "Syslog", Host = Computer, User = "", Image = SyslogMessage, Cmd = SyslogMessage, ParentImage = ProcessName, ParentCmd = "")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DNS lookup or TLS SNI for ShinyHunters azurenetfiles.net infrastructure AICommand & Control High
Detects DNS or TLS-SNI traffic referencing the azurenetfiles.net domain, which the article ties to the ShinyHunters TLS certificate served by the IOC IP set. The domain has no legitimate use and predates this campaign in prior ShinyHunters operations. Rationale: Article reports that several of the IOC IPs served a TLS certificate whose common name is azurenetfiles.net, and notes the domain has been previously linked to ShinyHunters. Any DNS resolution or TLS-SNI hit on this domain inside an enterprise is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against MITRE ATT&CK G1015 (ShinyHunters) and the BleepingComputer prior coverage that ties azurenetfiles.net to the group. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/oracle-peoplesoft-servers-hacked-in-shinyhunters-data-theft-attacks/ • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1015/ • https://threatfox.abuse.ch/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004 T1573
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel scrapers / sandbox detonations resolving the domain for telemetry
  • Researcher VMs or DFIR analysts manually nslooking up the IOC
  • URL filtering proxies pre-resolving categorisation lookups
  • Internal documentation tools that automatically resolve any URL strings pasted into tickets
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","NisSrv.exe","SenseIR.exe")
Response runbook
1. Triage: identify the querying host and the process that made the request — if it's a browser the lookup is likely a user clicking a phishing link; if it's a service or LOLBin it's likely C2. Cross-reference the source host against the seven IOC IPs from the network-traffic UC. 2. Contain: sinkhole or NXDOMAIN azurenetfiles.net (and its known subdomains) at the resolver, block all seven IOC IPs at the perimeter, and isolate the querying host pending triage. 3. Hunt: pull the full process tree on the querying host, look for MeshCentral binaries, SSH outbound to peer PeopleSoft systems, and the ransom-note filename across the estate.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "azurenetfiles.net" or RemoteUrl endswith ".azurenetfiles.net"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  (DnsEvents
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where Name has "azurenetfiles.net"
    | project TimeGenerated, _Source = "DnsEvents", Host = Computer, ClientIP, Query = Name, ResponseCode = ResultCode, Answer = Result),
  (ImDnsActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DnsQuery has "azurenetfiles.net"
    | project TimeGenerated, _Source = "ImDnsActivity", Host = SrcHostname, ClientIP = SrcIpAddr, Query = DnsQuery, ResponseCode = DnsResponseCodeName, Answer = DnsResponseName),
  (CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DestinationDnsDomain has "azurenetfiles.net" or RequestURL has "azurenetfiles.net" or DestinationHostName has "azurenetfiles.net"
    | project TimeGenerated, _Source = "CommonSecurityLog", Host = SourceHostName, ClientIP = SourceIP, Query = coalesce(DestinationDnsDomain, DestinationHostName, RequestURL), ResponseCode = EventOutcome, Answer = DestinationIP)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine

Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.

Cyber Security News
2026-06-10 6 use cases 2 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

Hackers are using fake tax notification emails to trick Windows users into downloading dangerous multi-stage malware that runs entirely in memory, leaving almost no trace behind. The campaign, tracked as Operation TaxShadow, has been active since at least May 20, 2026, targeting individuals by impersonating official Indian government tax authorities. Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;

    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)

              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)

| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,

SecurityEvent

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"

let BadHashes = dynamic(["185b7a487316454da04e9cc0fe6eb370bb2955cf6096fe3e8c02c46f8989ba37", "4c9061a07d667bf7dd6f597a43a8552af2f4277b7be06d6ea138abdb668d6a49", "949acbe543fc244ffbc981ea169067da7c5792af3c3d19b2c31b3d7e19106880", "be31a63cad112723178289968ad6f93a576c5a7984099c42eec3521cdf6e5fc0", "7d87a86dbd2379ef2516c99258137cd9c25ca19c48aeb096c5332c02fcbf16d0", "3a8f6454927b8993aded75de0de2bd00", "e83ff54e58f0b295a392c7fc39a7d0de", "b498256cb086a6962077cdd6d2f65327"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] JDY-style reconnaissance — internal host high-fanout mixed-protocol scanning · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] JDY Linux shell dropper — architecture-aware MIPS/MIPSEL payload retrieval
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] JDY botnet self-delete — Linux ELF executes then unlinks its own image · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
JDY Linux shell dropper — architecture-aware MIPS/MIPSEL payload retrieval AIInstallation High
Hunts for the JDY first-stage shell dropper behavior on Linux SOHO/IoT/edge hosts: a curl/wget/tftp invocation that pulls a payload whose URL or filename embeds one of the architecture tokens (mips, mips64, mipsel, mipsel64) the dropper uses to select the right binary. Highly article-specific because the dropper enumerates exactly this set. Rationale: Anchors on the exact architecture-token set the article calls out (mips, mips64, mipsel, mipsel64) inside a download tool's cmdline — a combination that doesn't appear in benign sysadmin/package-manager activity. Corroborated against Lumen Black Lotus Labs' KV-botnet writeup (same MIPS-router targeting) and BleepingComputer's reporting on the JDY expansion. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.lumen.com/kv-botnet-dont-call-it-a-comeback/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/china-linked-jdy-botnet-expands-targeting-of-us-military-networks/ • https://blog.lumen.com/routers-roasting-on-an-open-firewall-the-kv-botnet-investigation/
ATT&CKT1105 T1059.004 T1027.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • OpenWrt/DD-WRT firmware update scripts pulling MIPS images by architecture name
  • Embedded-systems developers cross-compiling/downloading test binaries for MIPS targets onto Linux jump hosts
  • Yocto/Buildroot CI workers fetching MIPS toolchains over HTTP
  • Network appliance vendor maintenance scripts that name-tag firmware by architecture
  • Researchers/reverse-engineers downloading public malware samples for analysis from MalwareBazaar/VX-Underground
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("apt","apt-get","dpkg","yum","dnf","opkg","pacman","zypper","snap")
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("apt","unattended-upgrades","buildroot","yocto")
Response runbook
Step 1 (Triage): Pull the parent process tree — confirm whether the curl/wget was launched by a legitimate package manager (apt/yum/opkg) or by an interactive shell / cron / unknown parent. Resolve the destination URL and check it against Black Lotus Labs' JDY IOC list on GitHub. Step 2 (Contain): If the host is a SOHO router, embedded device, or production server with no MIPS-development purpose, isolate from the network and snapshot for forensics — the binary self-deletes so capture /proc/<pid>/exe before kill. Step 3 (Hunt): Pivot on the destination IP/host across DeviceNetworkEvents (or ImNetworkSession) for the last 30 days to find sibling infections. Check for downstream high-fanout scanning from the host (UC #3).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("curl","wget","ftpget","tftp","busybox")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\b(mips64|mipsel64|mipsel|mips)\b"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("http://","https://","://",".onion")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FileName,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("curl","wget","ftpget","tftp","busybox")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\b(mips64|mipsel64|mipsel|mips)\b"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("http://","https://","://",".onion")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, Hash
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: JDY Botnet Linux Dropper - MIPS Architecture Payload Fetch
id: 8b5a4d1c-3f72-4e89-9b14-2e7c5f8a1d36
description: Detects the JDY botnet first-stage shell dropper retrieving an architecture-specific payload (mips/mipsel/mips64/mipsel64) via curl/wget/tftp/busybox on Linux SOHO/IoT hosts.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/china-linked-jdy-botnet-expands-to-1500.html
  - https://blog.lumen.com/kv-botnet-dont-call-it-a-comeback/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/10
tags:
  - attack.t1105
  - attack.t1059.004
  - attack.command_and_control
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_proc:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/curl'
      - '/wget'
      - '/ftpget'
      - '/tftp'
      - '/busybox'
  selection_arch:
    CommandLine|re: '(?i)\b(mips64|mipsel64|mipsel|mips)\b'
  selection_url:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'http://'
      - 'https://'
      - '.onion'
  condition: selection_proc and selection_arch and selection_url
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE (@process.name:(curl OR wget OR ftpget OR tftp OR busybox)) @process.command_line:(*mips* OR *mipsel* OR *mips64* OR *mipsel64*) @process.command_line:(*http\:\/\/* OR *https\:\/\/* OR *.onion*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 #event_platform=Lin
| ImageFileName=/(curl|wget|ftpget|tftp|busybox)$/i

JDY botnet self-delete — Linux ELF executes then unlinks its own image AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for the JDY post-execution defense-evasion behavior described in the article: the scanner binary is launched then deleted from disk so a live process has no on-disk backing file. Correlates a process-create on a non-system path with a delete of that same path within seconds. Rationale: The article explicitly states 'Once the malware is launched, it's deleted from disk' — a distinctive evasion the article calls out as a JDY characteristic. By joining process-create with same-path file-delete within a tight window, we surface this specific behavior on Linux hosts that ship Defender/ASIM telemetry without alerting on package-manager temp-file churn (filtered via the FP block). Cross-checked against: • https://blog.lumen.com/kv-botnet-dont-call-it-a-comeback/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/china-linked-jdy-botnet-expands-targeting-of-us-military-networks/
ATT&CKT1070.004 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Self-extracting installer shell archives (.run, makeself) in /tmp that extract → exec → cleanup
  • Ansible/Salt/Chef one-shot runners that drop a script in /tmp, execute, then remove
  • snapd / flatpak sandbox helpers in /var/run that are short-lived
  • CI runner ephemeral build steps inside /tmp/buildXXX
  • pip/npm post-install hooks that compile and clean up in /tmp
Suppression filter
| where ParentName !in~ ("sh","bash","dash") or true
| where not (ImagePath has_any ("/tmp/ansible-","/tmp/saltrun-","/tmp/build","/tmp/pip-","/tmp/npm-","/var/run/snapd/","/run/user/"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (Triage): For the matched process, dump /proc/<pid>/exe and /proc/<pid>/maps before the process exits — the deleted ELF is still mapped and can be recovered from memory. Capture the SHA256 and check against JDY samples on Black Lotus Labs' GitHub IOC repo. Step 2 (Contain): If recovered binary matches JDY tooling (or shows raw-socket SYN-scan code paths), isolate the host. Block any C2 IPs the live process is talking to (DeviceNetworkEvents → RemoteIP for that ProcessId). Step 3 (Hunt): Pivot on the parent process — JDY's dropper is a shell script; the parent should be /bin/sh or /bin/bash. Find the dropper invocation across the fleet and check for the architecture-specific payload pattern (UC #1).
let WindowSec = 30;
let ExecEvents = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FolderPath has_any ("/tmp/","/var/tmp/","/dev/shm/","/var/run/","/run/")
    | project ExecTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, AccountName,
              ImagePath = FolderPath, ImageName = FileName,
              SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, ParentName = InitiatingProcessFileName;
let DeleteEvents = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ActionType in ("FileDeleted","FileRenamed")
    | where FolderPath has_any ("/tmp/","/var/tmp/","/dev/shm/","/var/run/","/run/")
    | project DelTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, DelPath = FolderPath, DelName = FileName,
              DelInitiator = InitiatingProcessFileName;
ExecEvents
| join kind=inner DeleteEvents on DeviceId
| where ImagePath == DelPath and ImageName == DelName
| extend GapSec = datetime_diff('second', DelTime, ExecTime)
| where GapSec between (0 .. WindowSec)
| project ExecTime, DelTime, GapSec, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ImagePath, ImageName, SHA256, ParentName, DelInitiator, ProcessCommandLine
| order by ExecTime desc
let WindowSec = 30;
let ExecEvents = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ActingProcessName has_any ("/tmp/","/var/tmp/","/dev/shm/","/var/run/","/run/")
    | project ExecTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
              ImagePath = ActingProcessName, CmdLine = ActingProcessCommandLine,
              Hash;
let DeleteEvents = ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventType == "FileDeleted"
    | where TargetFilePath has_any ("/tmp/","/var/tmp/","/dev/shm/","/var/run/","/run/")
    | project DelTime = TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DelPath = TargetFilePath;
ExecEvents
| join kind=inner DeleteEvents on DvcHostname
| where ImagePath == DelPath
| extend GapSec = datetime_diff('second', DelTime, ExecTime)
| where GapSec between (0 .. WindowSec)
| project ExecTime, DelTime, GapSec, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ImagePath, Hash, CmdLine
| order by ExecTime desc
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:(EXECVE OR DELETE) @process.executable.path:(*/tmp/* OR */var/tmp/* OR */dev/shm/* OR */var/run/* OR */run/*) -@process.executable.path:*/snap/* -@process.executable.path:*/.cache/yarn/*
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 #event_platform=Lin ImageFileName=/^\/(tmp|var\/tmp|dev\/shm|var\/run|run)\//
| rename(field=ImageFileName, as=ExecPath)
| join({#event_simpleName=FileDeleted #event_platform=Lin TargetFileName=/^\/(tmp|var\/tmp|dev\/shm|var\/run|run)\//}, field=aid, key=aid, include=[TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName, _time], mode=inner)
| ExecPath = TargetFileName
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ExecPath], function=[count(), min(_time)])
ENDPOINT

| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_path IN ("/tmp/*","/var/tmp/*","/dev/shm/*","/var/run/*","/run/*") by _time host Processes.process_path Processes.process_name Processes.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | rename _time as procTime process_path as targetPath | join type=inner host targetPath [ | tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.action="deleted" Filesystem.file_path IN ("/tmp/*","/var/tmp/*","/dev/shm/*","/var/run/*","/run/*") by _time host Filesystem.file_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | rename _time as delTime file_path as targetPath ] | eval gapSec=delTime-procTime | where gapSec >= 0 AND gapSec <= 30 | table procTime delTime gapSec host user process_name targetPath

JDY-style reconnaissance — internal host high-fanout mixed-protocol scanning AIReconnaissance Medium
Detects a single internal host (likely a compromised SOHO/IoT device or jump box recruited into JDY) exhibiting the article's hallmark scanning shape: high-volume, simultaneous TCP/TLS/UDP/ICMP probing against many distinct external destinations in a short window. Tuned to fire on the rate + protocol-diversity + destination-fanout combination, which is the JDY tasking signature. Rationale: Article calls out the exact scanning shape: 'high-volume TCP, SSL, UDP, and ICMP-assisted probing' on the same node. Detecting that protocol mix combined with a fanout floor (200+ destinations, 20+ ports, <5 conn/dst mean) is far more article-specific than a generic 'noisy source' alert and is the JDY tasking signature. Corroborated against Lumen's KV-botnet writeup which describes identical mixed-protocol probing from the predecessor cluster. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.lumen.com/kv-botnet-dont-call-it-a-comeback/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/china-linked-jdy-botnet-expands-targeting-of-us-military-networks/ • https://blog.lumen.com/routers-roasting-on-an-open-firewall-the-kv-botnet-investigation/
ATT&CKT1595.002 T1046 T1584.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys/Rapid7 InsightVM/Tenable.io scan engines)
  • Internet measurement projects (Censys/Shodan-like scanners) running on a security research host
  • RUM/synthetic monitoring agents (Datadog, NewRelic) hitting many endpoints
  • MDM/EDR agents doing bulk policy refresh against many cloud endpoints
  • P2P clients on user laptops (BitTorrent DHT chatter looks similar)
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("nessus-scanner-01","qualys-engine-01","rapid7-engine-01")
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("scanner","probe","monitor"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (Triage): Identify the source DeviceName/SrcIpAddr — is it on the asset inventory? If yes, is it a sanctioned scanner (Nessus engine, internal probe)? Check OS/role: SOHO/IoT firmware, network appliance, IP camera, NVR are high-suspicion. Step 2 (Contain): If unsanctioned, network-isolate via NAC or 802.1X quarantine VLAN. For an IoT/SOHO device, power-cycle is rarely sufficient — JDY survives reboot per Lumen; pull the device and reimage. Step 3 (Hunt): Look for the dropper chain on this host (UC #1) and for outbound connections to Tor entry nodes from the same source. Pull DNS for the past 7 days from the host's resolver — JDY uses Tor relays as C2, so look for .onion lookups or known Tor consensus IPs.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1h)
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionAttempt","ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionFailed","InboundConnectionAccepted")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize 
    DistinctDsts = dcount(RemoteIP),
    DistinctPorts = dcount(RemotePort),
    DistinctProtos = dcount(Protocol),
    Protos = make_set(Protocol, 10),
    SamplePorts = make_set(RemotePort, 20),
    TotalConns = count()
    by DeviceName, DeviceId, bin(Timestamp, 5m)
| where DistinctDsts >= 200 and DistinctProtos >= 3 and DistinctPorts >= 20
| extend MeanConnsPerDst = TotalConns * 1.0 / DistinctDsts
| where MeanConnsPerDst < 5     // scanner shape: many destinations, few packets each
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where isnotempty(DstIpAddr) and DstIpAddr !startswith "10." and DstIpAddr !startswith "192.168." and DstIpAddr !startswith "172.16."
| summarize 
    DistinctDsts = dcount(DstIpAddr),
    DistinctPorts = dcount(DstPortNumber),
    DistinctProtos = dcount(NetworkProtocol),
    Protos = make_set(NetworkProtocol, 10),
    TotalConns = count()
    by SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where DistinctDsts >= 200 and DistinctProtos >= 3 and DistinctPorts >= 20
| extend MeanConnsPerDst = TotalConns * 1.0 / DistinctDsts
| where MeanConnsPerDst < 5
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationIp:* -@DestinationIp:(10.* OR 192.168.* OR 172.16.* OR 172.17.* OR 172.18.* OR 172.19.* OR 172.20.* OR 172.21.* OR 172.22.* OR 172.23.* OR 172.24.* OR 172.25.* OR 172.26.* OR 172.27.* OR 172.28.* OR 172.29.* OR 172.30.* OR 172.31.*)
#event_simpleName=/^NetworkConnectIP[46]$/
| ConnectionDirection=0 OR ConnectionDirection=1
| !cidr("10.0.0.0/8", field=RemoteAddressIP4) | !cidr("192.168.0.0/16", field=RemoteAddressIP4) | !cidr("172.16.0.0/12", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| bucket(span=5m, field=_time, function={ groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function=[count(as=Total), count(field=RemoteAddressIP4, distinct=true, as=DistinctDsts), count(field=RemotePort, distinct=true, as=DistinctPorts), count(field=Protocol, distinct=true, as=DistinctProtos)]) })
| DistinctDsts >= 200
| DistinctProtos >= 3
| DistinctPorts >= 20
